## How It Works

1. 01
 Discover
 One call to talk through your business, your customers, and what the site has to do — bookings, phone calls, or looking the part.
2. 02
 Plan
 Pages, content, and the path from landing to getting in touch. Every decision is made here, before a line is written.
3. 03
 Build
 Designed and built from scratch, around your business. Fast, because every decision was settled before it started.
4. 04
 Review
 You see the finished site and ask for changes. Nothing goes live until you're happy with it.
5. 05
 Launch
 Domain connected. Tested on desktop and phone. Live.

Not scaled-down agency work. Sites for plumbers, landscapers, detailers — any business that needs a call, a booking, or a walk-in. Not a brand campaign.

No account managers. No handoffs. No ticket queue. The person who answers your email writes the code.

One monthly fee, nothing up front. Quoted in a single conversation. No packages to decode, no surprises on the invoice.

Phones in bright sun. Keyboards instead of mice. Screen readers. The site is built and tested for all of it, to WCAG 2.1 AA — the accessibility standard courts apply to business websites.

Hosting, security, backups, and the small updates you'll want. Handled monthly. A year on, it still runs like it did on day one.

Work in progress, finished projects, the occasional look behind the build. Posted as it happens.

# Services — Websites From $97 a Month

Source: https://jtbuildsco.com/services

One number: $97 a month covers building your site, hosting it and keeping it up to date. No setup fee. Add-ons only if your business has a use for them.

## What It Costs

One fee covers the lot. Building the site, putting it online, and keeping it there.

MONTHLY FEE

### Everything, in one number

Starting at **$97** / month

No setup fee, no deposit, no contract. The build is included in the monthly, so you pay nothing before your site exists and nothing extra once it does.

- Design & build
- Accessibility
- Optimization
- Launch
- Hosting
- Security
- Backups
- Maintenance
- Content updates

**Nothing up front.** The build is inside the monthly fee rather than charged before it, so getting online costs one number instead of a lump sum and a bill. One number, not a menu.

## Optional Add-ons

Genuinely optional. Added only when your business has a use for them.

### Branding

A logo and typography that carry from storefront to screen — signage, cards, and packaging all speaking the same language.

### Booking

Appointments taken around the clock, straight from your site — no phone tag, no back and forth.

### Local Search

Google Business Profile setup and local SEO, so your town finds you first when they search for what you do. [How a Google Business Profile is set up](https://jtbuildsco.com/blog/google-business-profile-setup-massachusetts).

### AI & Custom Solutions

Automation, internal tools, missed-call text-back, review requests, e-commerce, and mobile apps to sit alongside your site — built around how your business actually runs.

### Advertising

Instagram and Google ads set up and running, with the graphics to go in them. Or I set them up, walk you through how they work, and hand you the controls.

**A website as a service, not a purchase.** Your words, your photos, your logo and your domain are yours throughout, and you can take them with you. The site itself stays with the studio and goes offline if the fee stops — there is no build cost to buy it out, because you were never charged one.

# Pricing

Source: https://jtbuildsco.com/pricing

One number, not a menu: $97 a month covers the build, the hosting and the upkeep. No setup fee, no contract, and the figure is agreed before anything starts.

## One Number

One fee covers the lot. Building the site, putting it online, and keeping it there.

MONTHLY FEE

### Everything, in one number

Starting at **$97** / month

No setup fee, no deposit, no contract. The build is included in the monthly, so you pay nothing before your site exists and nothing extra once it does.

- Design & build
- Accessibility
- Optimization
- Launch
- Hosting
- Security
- Backups
- Maintenance
- Content updates

**Nothing up front.** Most studios ask for a build fee of a few thousand dollars before they start. This is the same work, paid monthly instead, so the cost of getting online is a single number you can budget for. Add-ons like branding, booking, local search, and advertising are genuinely optional, and quoted on their own.

## Quoted, Not Packaged

No packages to decode, and no tiers named after metals. A site that changes weekly asks more than one that stands still, so the figure is quoted personally in a single consultation and agreed in writing before any work begins.

Anything outside what we agree is quoted first. Nothing is added to an invoice after the fact.

## Questions

### How long does a website take?

Days, not months. The consultation settles what the site needs to do, and once you sign off the build runs uninterrupted. The part that varies is how quickly you get me your photos and copy.

### Can you connect a domain I already own?

Yes. Connecting your domain and launching the site is included — you don't need to touch any settings yourself.

### What if I don't have a domain yet?

We'll sort one out together during the consultation — I'll help you choose it and get it registered. However it's bought, the domain is registered to your business and stays yours.

### What happens after my site launches?

Nothing changes and nothing else is due. The same monthly fee keeps it hosted, secure, backed up and maintained, and covers the small content updates you'll want — new photos, hours, prices, a few lines of copy. Month to month, with no lock-in.

### What if I need changes after launch?

Send them over. Minor updates — wording, photos, hours, prices — are part of the monthly fee, with no ticket system and no change fee. Anything substantially larger, like a redesign, a new page, or a new feature, is quoted separately before I start.

### Can the site include booking or contact forms?

Yes to both. A contact form that reaches you directly is standard; online booking is its own service, added where it fits how the business actually runs.

### Is SEO included?

The groundwork is: a fast, properly structured site that search engines can read, which is the part most small-business sites get wrong. Going further — Google Business Profile setup and local search work, so your town finds you first — is the Local Search service, agreed in your consultation.

### Do you set up text and call automation?

Yes, as an add-on — missed-call text-back and automated review requests, added when a business has a use for them rather than fitted to every site by default. If it's part of your project, it's built alongside the rest of the site.

Switching it on is a separate step. Before any business can text its customers, the phone carriers must verify its number — a registration that typically takes anywhere from a few days to a few weeks and can't be rushed by anyone. I file it at sign-off, and everything else launches while it clears.

### Do I own the website?

Not outright, and I'd rather say so plainly than bury it. This is a subscription: you're paying for a website that's built, hosted and looked after, the same way you'd pay Squarespace. There's no build fee, so nothing has been paid to buy it. Stop the subscription and the site comes offline.

What is yours stays yours, always. Your domain is registered to your business and points wherever you tell it. Your words, your photographs and your logo are yours, and I'll hand them back on request so you can use them anywhere. Your Google Business Profile is yours too — I'll set it up with you or hand you the keys, whichever you'd rather.

If owning the files outright matters to you, say so at the consultation. That's a different arrangement with a build fee attached, and it's a fair thing to want.

[Who owns the site once it is built](https://jtbuildsco.com/blog/who-owns-your-website-domain-hosting-access) takes the question apart properly — the domain, the hosting, the files and your content are four separate things, and you can check where you stand with any provider in about ten minutes.

### What if I have nothing yet — no logo, no photos?

Then we begin there. Identity and imagery can be part of the engagement. [What to have ready before you hire anyone](https://jtbuildsco.com/blog/what-to-have-ready-before-hiring-web-designer) lists what genuinely helps, and what can wait.

### Will my site be accessible?

Yes — it's part of the build, not an add-on. Colour contrast, keyboard navigation, visible focus, screen-reader labelling, and reduced-motion support are checked against WCAG 2.1 Level AA, the standard the Department of Justice and the courts apply to business websites. This site passes it with zero violations, and yours is built the same way.

Being straight about the limit: automated testing covers a portion of that standard, not all of it. It rules out the common failures — the ones accessibility demand letters are written about — rather than certifying a site as perfect for every visitor.

### Can you run ads for my business?

Yes, as an add-on — Instagram and Google. That covers the setup, the targeting, and the graphics that go in the ads. If you'd rather run them yourself, I'll set them up, show you how each part works, and hand you the login.

The ad budget is separate. You set it, and you pay Google or Meta directly — it never goes through me, and my fee doesn't include it. What ads cost to run is your call, not a number I quote.

### Do we need to meet in person?

No. Everything runs online. The consultation is a call, and drafts, revisions, and approvals go back and forth by email or text. It's quicker that way — no travel, nothing scheduled around a drive, and the build starts the moment you sign off.

### Do you work outside Massachusetts?

Yes, in all fifty states. The work is online either way, so being down the road from Foxboro or across the country changes nothing about how the project runs.

# About — JT Builds Co., Foxboro Web Design Studio

Source: https://jtbuildsco.com/about

Most local businesses don't lose a customer on quality. They lose them on looking less established than whoever the customer found first.

## What Actually Costs You the Client

By the time someone calls, they've usually already decided. They searched, compared a couple of options, and picked whichever one looked like the safer bet — an updated website, a real Google Business Profile, a presence that said *this business has its act together*. Not necessarily the better business. Just the one that looked more established.

That's the part that's hard to watch: good businesses, doing genuinely good work, losing new customers to newer, weaker competitors — not on price, not on craft, but on who showed up first in a search and looked more legitimate doing it.

## Why I Started This

I watched this happen up close, to a local business I was close to — one that did great work and had loyal customers, and still kept losing new ones to competitors that simply had a stronger presence online. Nothing about the work was worse. The website was.

JT Builds Co. exists to close that gap: not with a generic template that looks like everyone else's, but with a website, a Google Business Profile, and a digital presence built specifically to make an already-good business look as established as it actually is.

## The Mission

Help the local businesses actually doing good work stop losing customers to the ones that just look more established online.

JAKE — FOUNDER

## The Founder

JT Builds Co. is one person, start to finish — no account managers, no outsourced production, no template. Every site and every profile is built by the person you're actually talking to.

Based FOXBORO, MA

Meetings ONLINE

Works with TRADES & ANY SMALL BUSINESS

Builds SITES, LOGOS & MORE

## Tell me what your business is losing right now.

A short conversation is usually enough to see exactly where you're losing ground — and what fixing it looks like.

# Web Design in Foxboro, MA

Source: https://jtbuildsco.com/web-design-foxboro-ma

JT Builds Co. is based here — not a national agency with a Foxboro landing page, but a one-person studio in the same town as the businesses it builds for.

## The Customer Decides Before They Call

Someone in Foxborough needs a haircut, a driveway sealed, a car detailed. They search, they open the first two or three results, and they pick whichever one looks like the safer bet. That decision is made in about ten seconds, on a phone, before anyone calls you.

Most of the time the business that wins isn't the better one. It's the one with a current website, a filled-out Google Business Profile, and photographs of its own work instead of stock images. If you're losing new customers to a newer competitor doing weaker work, that's usually the whole explanation.

The town is spelled both ways, incidentally — *Foxborough* on the town charter, *Foxboro* on most signs and mailing addresses. Your customers search both. A site built here knows that; a template bought from three states away doesn't.

## What Being Local Actually Changes

The work runs online — the consultation, the drafts, the approvals. Being down the road changes what I know about your market, not where the work happens. It's quicker this way: nothing to schedule around a drive, and the build starts the moment you sign off.

**I know the search you're competing in.** I know these towns, who else comes up when someone searches for what you do, and what a customer here is weighing you against. A studio three states away is guessing at that.

**Your photographs should be real.** The biggest difference between a site that converts and one that doesn't is whether the pictures are your actual shop, your actual van, your actual work. Nothing here is stock. I'll tell you exactly what to shoot on your phone, and that's usually all it takes.

**You talk to the person building it.** No account manager, no offshore production team, no ticket queue. One person, start to finish — the same one who answers the phone.

## The Promise

One monthly fee, starting at $97. It covers the build, the hosting and the upkeep. Nothing to pay before we start.

JAKE — FOUNDER

## Questions

### Do you only work with businesses in Foxboro?

No. Foxboro is where the studio is based. Clients are served in all fifty states, and since everything runs online, the process is identical either way.

### What kinds of local businesses is this for?

Plumbers, landscapers, detailers, contractors — the trades where a customer picks one of three search results and never calls the other two. That's where the problem bites hardest, not where it stops. If you have a Google listing and no real website, or a website you're embarrassed to send people to, that's the situation this is built for, whatever the business does.

### Do we need to meet in person?

No. Everything runs online — the consultation is a call, and drafts, revisions, and approvals go back and forth by email or text. Nothing about the work needs a table, and it saves us both the travel. Call [(781) 248-9834](tel:+17812489834) or [send a note](https://jtbuildsco.com/contact) and we'll find a time.

### Will this help me show up on Google Maps?

That's the Local Search service — Google Business Profile setup, categories, service areas, and the connection between the listing and the site. It's agreed in the consultation rather than fitted to every project by default. [Getting found on Google Maps locally](https://jtbuildsco.com/blog/google-business-profile-setup-massachusetts).

# Terms & Conditions

Source: https://jtbuildsco.com/terms

LAST UPDATED — JULY 2026

These terms govern engagements between JT Builds Co. ("JT Builds Co.," "we," "us") and clients ("you"). By requesting a consultation or engaging us for services, you agree to the terms below.

## Our Services

We design and build websites, identities and logos, local search presence, booking systems, advertising, and related digital services for small businesses, as described on our Services and Pricing pages. The exact scope of any engagement is agreed personally, in a consultation, before work begins.

## Fees & Payment

An engagement is a single recurring monthly fee. It covers designing and building the site, hosting it, security, backups, technical maintenance, and minor content updates. There is no separate setup or build charge: the build is recovered through the monthly fee rather than billed before work starts. Substantial work beyond that — redesigns, additional pages, or new features — is quoted separately and agreed before it is carried out. Optional add-ons such as branding, booking, local search, and advertising are quoted on their own. Where we set up or run advertising, our fee covers that work only: the advertising budget itself is paid by you to Google or Meta directly, is set by you, and is not part of what you pay us. Exact pricing and payment terms are quoted and agreed during your consultation and confirmed in writing before work begins.

## What You Are Paying For

This is a subscription to a website, not a purchase of one. While the monthly fee is paid, your site is live, hosted, secured and maintained by us. There is no separate build fee, so nothing has been paid to buy the site outright.

Your own material remains yours throughout and is not affected by this agreement: the words you supply, your photographs, your logo, and your domain name, which is registered to your business. You can take all of it with you at any time.

The website itself — the design, the code, and the build we produce — remains the property of JT Builds Co. and is licensed to you for as long as the fee is paid.

The fee covers hosting, security, backups and technical maintenance, so that none of it falls to you to manage. It also covers minor content updates such as new photos, revised copy, pricing, and hours, carried out by us on request. Larger work, such as a redesign, additional pages, or new functionality, falls outside the monthly fee and is quoted separately before it is undertaken.

Your Google Business Profile is handled however you prefer: we can set it up and hand you the login, or manage it as part of your monthly fee. Specific access and handover arrangements for any engagement are confirmed with you directly.

## Your Responsibilities

You agree to provide accurate information and any content (photos, copy, logos, and so on) needed to complete your project, and to respond to requests for feedback or approval in a reasonably timely way, since delivery timelines depend on it.

## Cancellation

The monthly fee runs month to month and can be cancelled at any time with reasonable notice. There is no minimum term and no long-term contract.

Cancelling ends the subscription, and the website goes offline at the end of the period you have paid for. Because the build was never charged for separately, the site is not transferred and the files are not handed over.

What is yours stays yours. Your domain name points wherever you tell it to, and we will return your written content, your photographs and your logo on request so you can use them with another provider. We will not hold your domain or your own material.

## Limitation of Liability

We build and maintain your website and related services with care, but we don't guarantee specific business outcomes — such as a particular volume of leads, bookings, or sales — since those depend on many factors outside our control. We aren't liable for indirect or consequential losses arising from your use of the services.

## Changes to These Terms

We may update these terms from time to time. The date at the top of this page reflects the most recent revision. Material changes affecting an active engagement will be discussed with you directly.

## Governing Law

These terms are governed by the laws of the Commonwealth of Massachusetts.

## Contact

Questions about these terms can be sent to [jptwohig16@gmail.com](mailto:jptwohig16@gmail.com).

This page is provided for general information about how we work and isn't a substitute for legal advice.

# Privacy Policy

Source: https://jtbuildsco.com/privacy-policy

LAST UPDATED — AUGUST 2026

JT Builds Co. ("JT Builds Co.," "we," "us") operates this website and provides web design, branding, and related services to small businesses. This policy explains what information we collect from visitors and consultation requests, and how it's used.

## Information We Collect

When you submit the consultation form on this site, we collect what you choose to share: your name, business name, email address, phone number (if given), the services you're interested in, and any message you write. We don't collect payment information through this website — that's handled directly, by invoice, once an engagement begins.

## How We Use It

We use this information to respond to your inquiry, discuss your project, and, if we work together, to deliver and maintain the services you've engaged us for. We do not sell, rent, or trade your information to third parties for marketing purposes.

## Third-Party Services

The consultation form is processed by [FormSubmit](https://formsubmit.co/), a third-party form-delivery service and data processor that relays your submission to us by email — they receive what you type into the form, and act only on our behalf in delivering it. We also load typefaces from Google Fonts, which may receive your device's IP address as part of delivering font files, and send text messages on clients' behalf through Twilio, described below. We don't use analytics, tracking pixels, or advertising cookies on this site.

## Website Health Report Tool

Our Website Health Report tool, at [report.jtbuildsco.com](https://report.jtbuildsco.com/), lets a visitor enter any website's domain and get back an automated report on it. The domain you submit is fetched and analyzed on our server; the result is cached briefly — about 10 minutes — to speed up repeat lookups, and isn't stored permanently after that. We also use your IP address briefly, to prevent abuse and rate-limit requests; it isn't retained long-term.

## Text Messages Sent on a Client's Behalf

Some clients use our Reviews or Response service, which sends a one-time text to their own customer — for example, asking for a review once a job is finished, or replying to a missed call. If you've received one of these messages, it's because a business you did work with gave us your number for that purpose. We send it through Twilio, our messaging provider, and don't use the number for anything else. Reply STOP to any message to opt out.

## Client Content

If you engage us for ongoing website care, we may store the photos, text, and other materials you provide us in order to build and update your site. That content remains yours and is used only for the work you've asked us to do.

## Data Retention

We keep consultation and client information for as long as it's useful to our working relationship, or as needed to meet legal and accounting obligations. You can ask us to delete information we hold about you at any time, as described below.

## Your Rights

You can ask us, at any time, what information we hold about you, ask us to correct it, or ask us to delete it. Reach out using the contact details below and we'll take care of it directly.

## Children's Privacy

This site and our services are intended for business owners and are not directed at children under 13. We do not knowingly collect information from children.

## Changes to This Policy

We may update this policy from time to time as our practices change. The date at the top of this page reflects the most recent revision.

## Contact

Questions about this policy or your information can be sent to [jptwohig16@gmail.com](mailto:jptwohig16@gmail.com).

This page is provided for general information about how we handle data and isn't a substitute for legal advice.

# How to Set Up a Google Business Profile That Actually Ranks

Source: https://jtbuildsco.com/blog/google-business-profile-setup-massachusetts

[&larr; GUIDES](https://jtbuildsco.com/blog)

31 August 2026 · 7 min read

A step-by-step Google Business Profile setup guide for Massachusetts trades, salons and shops: categories, service areas, photos, reviews and suspension traps.

A Google Business Profile is free, takes about an hour to set up properly, and decides whether anyone within ten miles of you ever finds your business. For most Massachusetts trades, salons and shops it does more work than the website does. That is not an argument against websites. It is an argument for doing this first.

I set these up for clients alongside their sites, and the difference between a profile that ranks and one that does not is almost never effort. It is a handful of specific choices, made early, that are painful to reverse later. Here is how to make them correctly.

## What Google says it is measuring

Google publishes its own answer, and it is worth reading before you touch anything. Local ranking comes down to three things: relevance, distance and prominence ([Google Business Profile Help, "Improve your local ranking on Google"](https://support.google.com/business/answer/7091?hl=en)).

**Relevance** is how well your profile matches what somebody typed. **Distance** is how far you are from them, which you cannot change. **Prominence** is how well known your business is — review count, review scores, and links to your site from elsewhere on the web.

Google also states plainly that there is no way to pay for a better local ranking. Anyone who tells you otherwise is selling something.

That leaves you two levers: make the profile unmistakably relevant, and build prominence over time. Everything below serves one of those two.

## Step one: claim it before you build it

Search your business name plus your town. There is a reasonable chance a profile already exists — Google generates them from other data sources, and old ones linger from previous owners. Claiming an existing profile keeps whatever review history is attached to it. Creating a duplicate splits your history and eventually gets one of them suspended.

Verification usually happens by postcard, phone, email or video, and Google decides which. Video verification has become common for service-area businesses and it means recording your van, your tools, your signage and your work in one continuous take. Have that ready before you start rather than scrambling on the day.

## Step two: pick the primary category carefully

This is the single most consequential field on the profile, and it is the one most people rush.

Your **primary category** does most of the work in matching you to searches. Secondary categories help, but they carry far less weight. Choose the category that describes what you do, not what you aspire to do.

A few Massachusetts examples:

- A mobile detailer should be **Car detailing service**, not **Car wash**. Different search intent entirely.
- A barber cutting men's hair should be **Barber shop**, not **Hair salon**, even though both are technically true.
- A landscaper who mostly plows in winter should still lead with **Landscaper** and add **Snow removal service** as secondary.
- An electrician doing residential work should be **Electrician**, not **Contractor**.

Test it yourself. Search the term a customer would use, look at who appears in the map results, and check what category those businesses are using. If the top three all use one category and you have chosen another, you have your answer.

## Step three: address or service area, not both

Google treats these as different kinds of business, and getting it wrong is the most common cause of suspension.

If customers come to you — a salon, a shop, a garage — show your address. If you go to them — detailing, plumbing, landscaping, mobile services — hide the address and set a service area instead. Do not display a home address for a business customers never visit. Google's guidelines are explicit that your listed location has to be somewhere you are actually staffed during stated hours ([Google Business Profile Help, "Guidelines for representing your business on Google"](https://support.google.com/business/answer/3038177?hl=en)).

Keep the service area realistic. A detailer in Foxboro listing Foxborough, Mansfield, Walpole, Norton, Wrentham, Plainville and Sharon is credible. The same detailer listing all of Massachusetts is not, and the wider area does not help you rank further away — distance is measured from your actual location regardless.

## Step four: fill in every field, including the ones that seem pointless

Relevance is largely a function of completeness. Work through all of it:

- **Business name** exactly as it appears on your signage. Do not add keywords. "Clover Downs Detailing" is correct. "Clover Downs Detailing — Best Mobile Car Detailing Beverly MA" is a suspension waiting to happen.
- **Hours**, including holiday hours. Google surfaces "open now" heavily.
- **Services**, listed individually with short descriptions. Most businesses leave this empty. It is free relevance.
- **Attributes** — appointments required, wheelchair accessible entrance, women-owned, whatever applies.
- **Description**, 750 characters, written for a person rather than stuffed with town names.
- **Website link**, pointing at the most relevant page rather than always the homepage.
- **Opening date**, which is a small trust signal.

## Step five: photographs, and the reason yours matter more than you think

Photos are where most profiles are weakest and where the gap is easiest to close.

Upload your own. Your shop, your van, your team, your finished work. Not stock images, not manufacturer product shots. Ten good photos of real work beat forty generic ones, and a profile with no photos reads as abandoned.

Add a few every month. A profile that is being maintained looks different from one that was filled in once in 2023 and left, and customers can tell even if they could not explain how.

## Step six: reviews, asked for properly

Review count and score feed directly into prominence. Google says so.

Ask at the moment the customer is happiest, which is when you hand the work back, not three weeks later by email. Send them a direct review link rather than instructions. Respond to every review, including the bad ones, in a couple of sentences without arguing.

What you must not do: offer discounts or anything else in exchange for reviews, post reviews of your own business, or ask a friend who was never a customer. Google's guidelines prohibit incentivised reviews, and review filtering catches bursts of them.

Steady beats fast. Two genuine reviews a month for a year is a much better position than twenty in one week.

## Google Business Profile mistakes that get a listing suspended

Almost every suspension I have seen traces to one of these:

1. Keywords stuffed into the business name.
2. A virtual office, mailbox or coworking address used as a storefront.
3. A service-area business displaying a home address.
4. Duplicate profiles for the same location.
5. A business category that does not match what the business visibly does.
6. Fake or incentivised reviews.

Reinstatement is possible but slow, and you argue it with a form rather than a person. Not triggering it is enormously easier.

## Frequently asked questions

**How long does it take for a Google Business Profile to rank?** Verification takes days to a couple of weeks. Meaningful movement in the map results usually takes one to three months of a complete profile with steady reviews and photos. There is no way to accelerate it with payment.

**Do I need a website to have a Google Business Profile?** No. You can run a profile without one. But the website link is one of the few prominence signals you directly control, and a profile pointing at a real site converts far better than one pointing nowhere. More on whether you need a site at all

**Should I list my home address if I work out of my house?** No. Set a service area and hide the address. Displaying a home address you do not staff for customers is against Google's guidelines and is a common cause of suspension.

**How many categories should I choose?** One primary category chosen carefully, then only the secondary categories that genuinely describe services you offer. Adding unrelated categories dilutes relevance rather than broadening it.

**Can I set up a Google Business Profile myself?** Yes, entirely. It costs nothing and takes an hour or two if you have your photos and details ready. The reason people pay for it is the category and service-area decisions, and the reinstatement process if something goes wrong.

## Where to start

If you already have a profile and are not sure whether it is working, check the website it points to first — a profile sending traffic to a slow or broken site wastes the visibility it earns.

[Run a free Website Health Report on the site your profile links to](https://report.jtbuildsco.com/)

I set up and repair Google Business Profiles alongside the sites I build, across Massachusetts. [See how local search fits into a build](https://jtbuildsco.com/services) · [Or read how this works locally](https://jtbuildsco.com/web-design-foxboro-ma)

# What to Have Ready Before You Hire a Web Designer

Source: https://jtbuildsco.com/blog/what-to-have-ready-before-hiring-web-designer

[&larr; GUIDES](https://jtbuildsco.com/blog)

17 September 2026 · 6 min read

A practical checklist of what to have ready before hiring a web designer: content, photos, domain access, logins, and the questions worth asking first.

Nearly every website project that runs late runs late for the same reason. Not the design. Not the code. The content.

The designer finishes the layout in a few days, then sends an email asking for the About text, the service descriptions and some photos of the work. Three weeks pass. The owner is busy running a business, which is the entire reason they hired someone in the first place.

So here is what to have ready before you hire a web designer. Gather this first and the build is fast. Gather it afterwards and it is not.

## 1. The job the site has to do

One sentence. Not a mission statement.

"Get people to call for a quote." "Take bookings so I stop answering the phone during appointments." "Look established enough that commercial clients take me seriously." "Sell twelve products."

Everything else follows from this, and getting it wrong is the most expensive mistake available. A site built to take bookings looks different from a site built to win commercial contracts. If you cannot say it in a sentence, that is worth an hour of thinking before it is worth anyone's invoice.

## 2. Your words

You do not need to write finished copy. You do need to supply the raw material, because a designer inventing it produces something generic that sounds like every other site in your trade.

Have ready:

- **What you do**, in your own words, as you would say it on the phone.
- **The list of services**, each with two or three sentences.
- **How you are different** from the two competitors you lose work to. Be specific. "Quality and service" is not an answer.
- **Your story**, briefly. How long, why you started, what you did before.
- **The questions customers always ask.** Every one. These become your FAQ section, and they are the most useful thing you can hand over.
- **Prices**, or a decision about whether to show them.

Voice memos are fine. Talking is faster than writing and it sounds more like you.

## 3. Your photographs

The single biggest difference between a site that converts and one that does not is whether the pictures are real.

Your shop. Your van. Your team. Your finished work, before and after. Photographed on your phone in good light, which is usually outdoors on an overcast day or near a window.

Twenty real photos beat two hundred stock images. If you have none, say so early — a good designer will tell you exactly what to shoot, and it is usually an hour of your time.

Also have your **logo** in the highest quality file you can find. If the only copy you have is a JPEG pulled off Facebook, mention it now rather than at launch.

## 4. Your domain, and access to it

This is where projects get genuinely stuck.

Find out **who registered your domain and where**. GoDaddy, Namecheap, Google Domains, Wix, whoever. Then confirm you can log into that account yourself.

If a previous designer registered it for you, this is the moment to find out whether it is in your name — the registrant on record is the party with control, and transfers follow a published process ([ICANN, "Transferring Your Domain Name" registrant guidance](https://www.icann.org/resources/pages/transferring-your-domain-name-2017-10-10-en)). Sometimes it is not, and sorting that out takes weeks. Better to discover it now than the day before launch. [What to do if the domain is not in your name](https://jtbuildsco.com/blog/who-owns-your-website-domain-hosting-access)

If you have no domain at all, that is simpler. Have two or three names in mind.

## 5. Every login you can find

Make a list. You will need more of these than you expect:

| Account | Why it matters |
|---|---|
| Domain registrar | To point the domain at the new site |
| Current hosting | To retrieve content and shut it down cleanly |
| Google Business Profile | To link the new site and update information |
| Booking software | To embed or migrate the booking flow |
| Email provider | So business email keeps working through the switch |
| Social accounts | For linking and consistent details |
| Analytics, if any | To keep historical data |

Put them somewhere secure before the project starts. Hunting for a hosting password mid-launch is how a site goes down for a day.

## 6. Two or three sites you like, and why

Send links. More usefully, send a sentence with each explaining what you like — the layout, the colours, the way they explain their pricing, the photography.

"I like this one" tells a designer nothing. "I like how this one puts the phone number in the corner on every page" tells them everything.

Competitor sites are worth including too, including the ones you dislike. Knowing what you want to avoid is as useful as knowing what you want.

## 7. Your questions, asked before you sign

Five that matter more than the price:

1. **Who actually builds it?** Is the person quoting you the person doing the work?
2. **What is the turnaround, and what happens if it slips?** Get a number and a consequence.
3. **What happens after launch?** Who fixes it, how fast, and at what cost.
4. **Who owns the domain, the hosting and the code?** The answer should be you.
5. **Will it be built to accessibility standards?** Almost nobody asks. Why it is worth asking

And one for yourself: can you reach this person directly, or are you going through an account manager? For a small business, that difference shows up every time you need something changed.

## What you do not need to have ready before hiring a web designer

Some relief.

You do not need to know what pages the site should have — that is the designer's job. You do not need colours picked, a written brief, a sitemap, or any technical decisions about hosting or platforms. You do not need professional photography for most local businesses. And you do not need everything perfect before you start, only gathered.

## Frequently asked questions

**What should I prepare before hiring a web designer?** The job the site has to do in one sentence, your service descriptions and the questions customers always ask, real photographs of your work, your logo file, your domain and hosting logins, and two or three example sites you like with reasons.

**How long does a small business website take to build?** The build itself is usually days. Most projects take weeks because they are waiting on content from the owner. Having your text, photos and logins ready before you start is the single biggest thing you control.

**Do I need to write the content for my website myself?** Not the finished copy, but you should supply the raw material — what you do, how you describe it on the phone, and the questions customers ask. A designer writing from nothing produces generic text that sounds like every other site in your industry.

**What questions should I ask a web designer before hiring them?** Who actually builds it, what the turnaround is and what happens if it slips, what support looks like after launch and what it costs, who owns the domain and hosting, and whether the site will be built to accessibility standards.

**What if I do not have a logo or any photos?** Say so upfront. Logos can be designed as part of the project, and most local businesses can shoot everything they need on a phone in about an hour with a bit of direction.

## Before you gather anything, check what you already have

If you have an existing site, run it through the free Website Health Report first. It will tell you in plain English what is working and what is not, which usually clarifies whether you need a rebuild or a repair.

[Run a free Website Health Report](https://report.jtbuildsco.com/)

Then, when you are ready, tell me what your business does and what the site needs to accomplish. [Request a free consultation](https://jtbuildsco.com/contact) · [Or read who you would be working with](https://jtbuildsco.com/about)

Tell me what your business needs and I'll reply personally within one business day.

[REQUEST A FREE CONSULTATION](https://jtbuildsco.com/contact)

# Who Owns Your Website? Domain, Hosting and Access Explained

Source: https://jtbuildsco.com/blog/who-owns-your-website-domain-hosting-access

[&larr; GUIDES](https://jtbuildsco.com/blog)

17 September 2026 · 8 min read

Who really owns your website, domain and hosting, how to check it yourself in ten minutes, and exactly what to do if a web designer will not give you access.

The worst phone call in this trade is the one that starts "my old web guy has stopped answering, and I can't get into my own site."

It happens more than it should. Search around and you will find the same story in forums, on Reddit, on Quora, from owners of restaurants and clinics and contracting firms who paid for a website and discovered years later that they did not own it. Sometimes it is malice. More often it is convenience — the designer registered everything under their own account because it was faster, and then they moved on, or the relationship soured, or they simply disappeared.

You can find out where you stand in about ten minutes. Do that today, whoever built your site, including if it was me.

## Who owns your website? It is four separate things

This is the part nobody explains, and it is why the question gets confusing.

**The domain name.** Your address — the thing you rent from a registrar for about $15 a year. GoDaddy, Namecheap, Cloudflare, Squarespace. Whoever's name is on that registration controls it.

**The hosting.** The computer your site lives on, rented monthly. Separate account, often a different company entirely.

**The files and design.** The actual site — the code, the layout, the images. Who owns these depends on your contract, and often nobody wrote one.

**The content.** Your text, your photographs, your logo. Yours by default in most cases, though a photographer or designer may hold rights to specific work.

They can each be held by a different party. The domain is the one that matters most, because whoever controls it can point your web address anywhere, including nowhere.

## Check it yourself, right now

Four checks. None require technical skill.

**One: run a WHOIS lookup.** Search "WHOIS lookup," enter your domain, and look at the registrant. Privacy protection may hide the details, in which case note the registrar name and move to check two.

**Two: log into the registrar.** Go to whichever registrar came back, and try to log in with an email address you control. If you cannot, you have your answer.

**Three: check the billing.** Whose card renews the domain and the hosting each year? If it is not yours, somebody else holds the account.

**Four: log into the site itself.** Can you reach an admin area and change a phone number without asking anyone? If the only way to change your own hours is to email somebody, you have access, not control.

If all four come back clean, you are fine. Put a reminder in your calendar for the domain renewal date and get on with your day.

## What good looks like

The arrangement you want is simple, and any decent designer will set it up this way without being asked.

- The domain is registered **in your business's name**, with **your email** as the account contact, on **your card**.
- The hosting is in your name, or, if it is bundled into a monthly fee, the arrangement says in writing what happens to the site if you stop paying.
- You have admin access to your own site.
- Your content is yours, in writing.
- There is a written answer to "what happens if we part ways."

Hosting being bundled is normal and usually sensible — most owners do not want to manage a server. Bundling is fine. Bundling with no written answer to "what happens if I leave" is not.

The domain is the line I would not cross. Register it yourself, in your own name, before you hire anybody. It costs about $15 and it removes the entire problem permanently.

## Renting or owning: both are fine, if you are told

There are two honest ways to sell a website, and the difference is rarely explained to the person paying.

**You buy it.** You pay a build fee, the files are yours, and you can move the site to any host you like. This is the traditional arrangement. The build fee is usually a few thousand dollars, paid before the site exists.

**You subscribe to it.** You pay monthly, and that fee covers building the site, hosting it and looking after it. It stays online while you keep paying. Squarespace, Wix and Shopify all work this way. So does this studio: nothing is charged up front, and if the subscription stops, the site comes down.

Neither is a trick. Renting a website is not worse than buying one, any more than leasing a van is worse than buying one — it is a different way of spreading the same cost, and for an owner who would rather not find three thousand dollars in one go, it is often the better answer.

What matters is that you know which one you are in before you agree to it, and that your domain and your own material are yours either way. If a studio cannot answer "what happens to the site if I stop paying?" in one plain sentence, that is the problem. The answer itself is not.

## If you are already locked out

It is recoverable more often than people assume. In order:

**Ask plainly, in writing.** Email, not a phone call, so there is a record. Request the domain transfer authorisation code, the registrar and hosting account details, and admin access to the site. Set a date. Many cases resolve here — the designer is busy, not hostile.

**Check your contract and your invoices.** If a contract exists, it may already say the domain is yours. Invoices showing you paid for domain registration are useful evidence.

**Go to the registrar directly.** If the registration is in your business's name but you cannot access the account, the registrar has a recovery process and can help. Domain transfers between registrars follow a published process that every registrar has to honour ([ICANN, "Transferring Your Domain Name" registrant guidance](https://www.icann.org/resources/pages/transferring-your-domain-name-2017-10-10-en)). If it is in the designer's name, the registrar will not simply hand it over — it belongs to the registrant.

**Get a lawyer's letter.** Often less expensive than people expect, and frequently enough on its own. I am not a lawyer and this is not legal advice — if real money or a long-established domain is involved, speak to one properly.

**Consider the nuclear option.** If the domain is genuinely gone and recovery would take months, a new domain and a rebuilt site can be faster and cheaper. You lose search history and printed materials go stale, which is a real cost. Sometimes it is still the right call. What a rebuild costs in Massachusetts

What not to do: stop paying and hope. An expired domain can be bought by anybody, including someone who will sell it back to you for a great deal more than $15.

## Why this became normal

Worth saying, because the villain framing is usually wrong.

Most designers who hold client domains are not planning anything. They set up a registrar account years ago, put everything in it because it was one login instead of forty, and never thought about it again. The problem is structural rather than malicious. It only becomes a problem when the relationship ends — and relationships end for ordinary reasons like retirement, illness, or a career change.

Which is the point. A good arrangement should survive the designer disappearing. Mine is set up so that if I stopped answering the phone tomorrow, every client would still hold their own domain, their own words and their own photographs, and could put them in front of another builder the same afternoon. The site I built stays with me, because it was never sold — but nothing that belongs to them is ever tangled up with me.

That is not generosity. It is the minimum. [Why I run it this way](https://jtbuildsco.com/about)

## Frequently asked questions

**Who owns my website if someone else built it?** It depends on four separate things — the domain registration, the hosting account, the site files, and your content — and they can be held by different parties. Check the WHOIS registrant on your domain and whether you can log into the registrar and hosting accounts yourself.

**My web designer will not give me access to my website. What can I do?** Request the domain authorisation code and account access in writing with a deadline. Check your contract and invoices for evidence of ownership. Contact the registrar directly, which can help if the registration is already in your business's name. A lawyer's letter is often the next step and frequently resolves it.

**How do I find out who owns my domain name?** Run a free WHOIS lookup on your domain and check the registrant details. If privacy protection hides them, note the registrar and try to log into that registrar with an email address you control.

**Should my web designer register my domain for me?** It is fine for them to do it on your behalf, but it should be registered in your business's name with your email as the account contact. If it is registered in the designer's name, you do not control your own web address.

**What happens to my website if my web designer disappears?** If you hold the domain and hosting accounts, very little — another developer can take over. If the designer holds them, your site can go offline when the accounts lapse and recovery can take weeks. This is the reason to check before there is a problem.

If you are not sure what condition your current site is in, or who is hosting it, start with the free Website Health Report. It reads any business's site and explains the results in plain English.

[Run a free Website Health Report](https://report.jtbuildsco.com/)

And if you have decided to move on from a site you cannot control, I can tell you honestly whether it is worth rebuilding.
